description: Seven generations of Buendías in Macondo. García Márquez blends wonders and tragedy to tell the history of Latin America.

hero.hook: A rain of yellow flowers, a woman rising into the sky: the marvelous told as ordinary fact.

blocks.text: Published in **1967**, [[One Hundred Years of Solitude]] is the book that carried [[Magical realism]] to the world. That style presents magical events with the same calm as real ones, without surprise and without explanation. **Gabriel García Márquez**, born in **1927** and dead in **2014**, traces seven generations of the Buendía family in **Macondo**, a fictional village based on his hometown.

Political violence, economic imperialism, and ancestral myth are woven together. By breaking the straight line of time, the author lets wonder and tragedy live side by side with disconcerting ease. A rain of yellow flowers or a woman rising into the sky is reported as an ordinary fact.

**Gabriel García Márquez**, known as “Gabo,” drew on **Aracataca**, his Colombian hometown. His grandfather told him about the civil wars. His grandmother told him about ghosts and omens with an unshakeable seriousness. That way of reporting the marvelous without commenting on it became the key to his style.

blocks.caption: Gabriel García Márquez, the Nobel winner who made the world listen to Latin America

blocks.text: In **1965**, García Márquez had his flash of insight while driving to Acapulco. He turned the car around and shut himself away for 18 months to write, while his wife pawned their belongings.

The first print run of **8,000 copies** sold out in a few days in Buenos Aires. The author would receive the **Nobel Prize in literature** in **1982**, crowning a novel that had become the emblem of a whole continent of writing.

sections.title: The making of a style: Aracataca and the flash of insight

blocks.text: **José Arcadio Buendía** founds Macondo in the Colombian jungle. The village passes through ages: innocence, technology brought by gypsies, then political corruption. **Colonel Aureliano Buendía** leads thirty-two armed uprisings and loses every one. He embodies the tragic repetition of Latin American history.

blocks.caption: Macondo: a tropical village where the history of Latin America is condensed

blocks.text: The banana company that arrives in Macondo stands for the [[United Fruit Company and the "banana republics"]] of Central America, and the novel transposes the real **1928** banana massacre in Colombia. Thousands of striking workers are shot, and then a deluge washes away all memory of the event. García Márquez shows how economic imperialism and collective forgetting destroy a people.

sections.title: Macondo, between mythic founding and brutal reality

blocks.text: When **Remedios the Beauty** rises into the sky while folding sheets, the narrator shows no surprise at all. The magical is an organic extension of the real, not a decoration. That is the golden rule of [[Magical realism]]: the marvelous is part of daily life.

Time in Macondo is **circular**. The Buendías repeat the mistakes of their ancestors, reuse the same first names, and fall into the same passions. The manuscript of **Melquíades**, written in [[Sanskrit]], the coded language of the prophecies, tells the family's history a hundred years in advance. When it is finally read, a cyclone destroys Macondo and the circle closes.

sections.title: The machinery of the strange and the circle of time

blocks.text: The novel opened the way for the Latin American “**Boom**.” That literary movement marked the years **1960** to **1970**. Writers such as [[Mario Vargas Llosa]] belong to it. The novel proved that storytelling could carry a modern mythology as powerful as anything from antiquity.

García Márquez shows idealism eroded by war and by collective forgetting. Without memory and without solidarity, civilizations are short-lived, condemned to repeat their tragedies. Macondo is not only a village. It is a condensed Latin American memory, where the marvelous and the political touch.
The [[Magical realism]] of García Márquez uses the marvelous to tell the historical truth and the tragic solitude of Latin America.

subject: litterature
title: One Hundred Years of Solitude, García Márquez
